children: By Fabiana Negrin Ochoa and Ying Xian Wong
BANGKOK--Bank Indonesia has been given a widened mandate that includes growth. But its top priority is still stability, the central bank's newly minted governor said.

"I just want to stress that the main mandate for Bank Indonesia is still stability," Destry Damayanti said Thursday on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group meetings in Bangkok.
It is the first time she has attended the annual event as governor of Indonesia's central bank, having been tapped for the role in July and officially appointed in September.

So far this year, Bank Indonesia has delivered three interest-rate hikes--including one off-cycle move and an outsized 50-basis-point increase--aiming to tame flaring inflation and steady a volatile rupiah.
Since Destry has been at the helm, first as acting governor and then as governor, the bank has remained on hold, assessing the lagged impacts of prior tightening.

On Thursday, she declined to hint at what BI might do at its next meeting later this month, but said the 100 basis points of monetary tightening delivered in May and June could be enough to anchor inflation expectations and support rupiah stability.
She reiterated the bank's stance that its rate decisions are data-dependent.

If the global situation deteriorates, then maybe BI would see a case to deploy more policy ammunition, but right now it is focused on creating an "economic climate conducive to real growth and job creation."
Step one is to make sure that there is stability, Destry said, then low inflation and a steady currency.
The fallout from the U.S.-Iran war has hurt the oil-sensitive rupiah, which has weakened about 7% against the dollar so far this year.
BI has stepped in aggressively to support the currency, using various foreign-exchange intervention tools.
It still has "solid" forex reserves at its disposal, Destry said.
She noted that the rupiah's depreciation is in line with that of other emerging market peers, which for BI is more important than a specific level.
If other emerging-market currencies were moving in one direction and the rupiah in another, then "that means we have to do something stronger," she said.
